title: Extraction Methods and Innovations for Lithium, Cobalt, Nickel, and Manganese Metals from Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Abstract The remarkable growth of the electric vehicle sector has brought about an increasing number of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). This development presents an important opportunity to promote efficient and sustainable methods for the extraction and recycling of valuable metals, such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese. Traditional recycling techniques, including pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy, face certain challenges, such as high energy consumption, potential environmental impacts, and limitations in metal recovery efficiency. Considering these challenges, this study seeks to explore a range of extraction methods, contrasting traditional approaches with innovative sustainable alternatives such as bio-extraction and microbial metal recovery, which are aligned with the principles of a circular economy. This review aims to provide a thoughtful analysis of various selective extraction methods, outlining the strengths and weaknesses of each in relation to sustainable development and circular economic practices. Furthermore, it emphasizes the significant paradigm shift toward biotechnological solutions, particularly bioleaching, which offers promising environmental advantages. The adoption of sustainable extraction technologies is vital for enhancing the global recycling efficiency of LIBs. This approach not only aims to mitigate supply chain risks for essential battery metals but also reduces reliance on primary mining, thereby supporting broader efforts toward decarbonization and sustainability on a global scale. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The increasing growth of the electric vehicle (EV) sector is one of the key components in the global strategy for decarbonisation and the transition to sustainable transport systems [ 1 ]. However, the sustainability of this transition depends on securing a circular supply chain for critical metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are the principal energy storage technology powering EVs owing to their high energy density, lightweight design, and long cycle life [ 2 ,  3 ]. However, with the increasing distribution of EVs across the world, the number of end-of-life (EOL) EV batteries is projected to increase in the coming decades. This impending surge in LIB waste presents major environmental, economic, and resource challenges if not managed correctly [ 4 ]. Recycling spent LIBs is essential to reduce excessive extraction of raw material in the mining sector, which is energy-intensive and environmentally harmful. Recycling can recover up to 95% of key metals from LIBs, lowering carbon footprints [ 5 ]. Recycling also assists in mitigating supply chain risks, such as geopolitical tensions and supply shortages of cobalt from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) [ 6 ]. Reusing metals cuts emissions by 50–70% compared with primary extraction [ 7 ]. There are countries around the world that are accelerating the adoption of new energy vehicle (NEVs) under net-zero pledges, which include the European Union (EU) Green Deal, which mandates 50% Li-ion battery recycling efficiency by 2027, China’s NEV 2035 Plan, which prioritizes a closed-loop battery economy, and the US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which incentivizes domestic battery recycling to cut reliance on foreign supplies [ 8 ,  9 ].

Decarbonisation agendas include the Paris Agreement (2015), which drives EV adoption to cut transport emissions (30% of global CO 2 ), and the EU’s Circular Economy Action Plan, which enforces battery passport systems for traceability. These show that metal extraction and recycling from spent LIBs is vital for a sustainable NEV transition, aligning with global decarbonisation frameworks. Electric vehicle batteries rely on high value metals which form the cathode material, such as lithium (Li), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), and manganese (Mn), which are important for renewable energy systems, catalysis and manufacturing of new batteries, which sustain the EV industrial growth [ 10 ]. These transition metals are favored in cathodes owing to their ability to stabilize layered oxide structures, e.g., LiCoO 2  (lithium cobalt oxide) and LiNiMnCoO 2  (lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide), and provide high redox activity, which enhances energy density and cycling stability [ 11 ]. They are electrochemically important in EV battery manufacturing because lithium provides the fundamental charge carrier Li +  (lithium ions) owing to its low atomic weight and high reduction potential [ 12 ]. Cobalt in layered LiCoO 2  offers structural stability and high operating voltage but faces supply chain constraints [ 13 ]. Nickel in lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) and lithium nickel cobalt aluminum oxide (NCA) cathodes increases capacity but requires stabilization with Co and Mn to mitigate cation mixing [ 14 ]. Manganese enhances thermal safety and reduces cost but suffers from Mn dissolution at high voltages [ 15 ].

The extraction of these metals through mining is energy-intensive, including 15,000 kWh/ton lithium for brine processing, and this has been linked to ecological degradation, including groundwater depletion in lithium-rich salars in the Atacama Desert in Chile [ 16 ,  17 ,  18 – 19 ]. Lithium, vital for its lightweight and rechargeability [ 20 ], faces surging demand with 33% growth in extraction causing water shortages and pollution, especially in South America [ 1 ,  19 ]. The need to design out waste is critical; therefore, innovative solutions and initiatives are required to reduce the freshwater usage in the mining of lithium for a more circular approach [ 21 ]. Cobalt, largely sourced from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), involves artisanal mining (15–20%) with human rights risks, and its demand rose to about 20%, but recycling and low-cobalt batteries such as NMC and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) may ease pressure [ 22 ]. On the other hand, nickel demand is driven by high-energy cathodes, with Indonesia as the top producer, but mining causes deforestation [ 23 ,  24 ]. Copper, though 70% recycled, faces future shortages, with Indigenous lands holding key deposits, other metals such as manganese and iron, also pose environmental risks [ 23 ,  25 ,  26 ]. Thus, sustainable practices and recycling are critical to meet the demand for renewable energy technologies [ 27 ] and the development of a one-size-fits-all recycling method. A number of technologies have been developed, and some are under research for the extraction of these metals from spent EV batteries, each with distinct operational mechanisms, efficiencies, and challenges [ 28 ]. Pyrometallurgy is a process that uses high temperatures to melt shredded LIBs. It can achieve high recovery rates for certain metals such as cobalt, but other metals, particularly lithium, present more challenges and have low recovery rates, as a result.

Hydrometallurgy offers high recovery for lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese, with lower energy consumption compared with pyrometallurgy [ 29 ]. Challenges with hydrometallurgy include the consumption of large volumes of chemicals, management of liquid effluents, and process optimization for different battery chemistries such as NMC, NCA, and LFP [ 30 ]. Direct recycling is a developing method that focuses on recovering intact cathode materials from spent LIBs without disintegrating them into their constituent metals. This method could significantly reduce energy inputs and material losses compared to metallurgical methods [ 31 ]. However, it faces challenges including the need for precise sorting of battery chemistries, variations in battery designs, the degradation of active materials, and a lack of standardized manufacturing practices across EV manufacturers globally [ 32 ]. Scientists are exploring innovative extraction methods for metals from EV batteries, including electrochemical recovery methods, bio-metallurgy (bioleaching), and green solvents [ 33 ]. These methods aim to minimize chemical usage and secondary waste while enhancing metal recovery efficiencies [ 34 ].

However, challenges remain, such as the complexity of battery compositions, the economic feasibility of recycling operations, energy consumption, the environmental impact of process chemicals, and a lack of universal regulatory frameworks for battery recycling infrastructure [ 32 ]. Recovered metals are primarily reintroduced into the manufacturing of new EV batteries, supporting the circular economy and reducing dependence on primary resource extraction [ 32 ,  35 ]. High-purity nickel, cobalt, and manganese are critical for formulating advanced cathode materials, while lithium can be used in producing lithium salts for new battery cells [ 35 ]. Some recovered materials are used in the production of alloys, catalysts, and other electronic components [ 36 ].

While traditional pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy remain the industrial standard, they are limited by high energy consumption and secondary waste. This research goes a step further by offering a distinct sustainability-oriented framework based on the circular economy and bio-innovation that uses green solvents and microbes. This innovates around bio-extraction and cross-industry reuse, with extracted metals used in batteries and nonbattery applications sectors. This review is centered on a comprehensive paradigm shift toward a circular economy and evaluates how recovered metals can be repatriated to non-battery industries such as oil and gas, and renewable energy. Furthermore, it offers a detailed exploration of green leaching technologies, including deep eutectic solvents (DES), ionic liquids, and mechanochemical-assisted extraction. The review devotes more attention to bio-extraction mechanisms and serves as a strategic guidebook for global sustainability, aligning recycling methods with circular-economy principles and mitigating geopolitical supply-chain risks for cobalt and lithium. Most importantly, the research notably contributes to bridging the gap between laboratory-scale innovations and industrial reality, providing a roadmap for high-purity metal repatriation across diverse sectors, including renewable energy and oil and gas.

sections.heading: Types of LIBs and Their Composition
paragraphs: Research on rechargeable LIBs began in the 1960s, with the earliest examples being a CuF 2 /Li battery developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in 1965 [ 37 ]. British chemist M. Stanley Whittingham developed the earliest form of the modern Li-ion battery in 1974, using titanium disulfide (TiS 2 ) as a cathode material [ 38 ]. Initially, lithium metal anodes were abandoned owing to safety concerns, leading to the development of an intercalation anode to prevent the formation of lithium metal during battery charging [ 39 ]. Jürgen Otto Besenhard demonstrated lithium-ion reversible intercalation into graphite anodes in 1974, but later, Rachid Yazami used a solid organic electrolyte, polyethylene oxide, which was more stable [ 40 ,  41 ]. In the 1990s, significant improvements in energy density were achieved by replacing Yoshino’s soft carbon anode with hard carbon and later with graphite [ 40 ,  41 – 42 ]. Jeff Dahn and other researchers at Dalhousie University reported reversible intercalation of lithium ions into graphite in the presence of ethylene carbonate solvent, which represented the final innovation of the era that created the basic design of the modern LIBs [ 43 ].

Batteries with NMC chemistry are the most commonly used in the automotive sector. Using the NMC chemistry, high specific energies of up to 220–240 Wh/kg can be achieved [ 52 ]. This is a clear, decisive competitive advantage because it allows a large amount of energy to be stored with a low weight and volume and this allows more energy to be installed in the vehicle compared with other lithium-based technologies [ 53 ,  54 – 55 ]. There are various types of NMC chemistry, which include NMC 111 (nickel 33.3%–manganese 33.3%–cobalt 33.3%), NMC 622 (nickel 60%–manganese 20%–cobalt 20%), and NMC 811 (nickel 80%–manganese 10%–cobalt 10%) [ 56 ,  57 ]. NMC 811 materials are the newest and have a high nickel concentration and a very low manganese and cobalt content, which results in higher energy density at a lower cost [ 58 ]. The more common are the NMC 622 cells found in modern EVs such as those from Tesla and Bayerische Motoren Werke (BMW) as a balance between energy, cost, and longevity [ 59 ]. It is therefore clear that NMC technology, in its evolution, has set itself a goal of reducing cobalt as much as possible, but this is still at laboratory phase, because cobalt is an element that gives stability to the system and increases life cycles [ 30 ,  60 ]. However, there are companies experimenting with innovative new technologies such as Svolt Energy Technology in China, which recently announced the first NMX cell with dopants or modifiers engineered to compensate cobalt [ 61 ]. Each cathode chemistry has distinct characteristics that affect its performance, cost, safety, and recyclability [ 62 ]. LCO (lithium cobalt oxide) has a high cobalt content (17.3%) but moderate lithium content (2%). It was dominant in early EVs owing to its high energy density [ 35 ,  63 ]. It is expensive and ethically contentious owing to cobalt sourcing and has lower thermal stability, posing safety risks if damaged [ 35 ,  63 ]. Lithium iron phosphate is iron-rich (43.2%), with no cobalt or nickel, and its lithium content is modest (1.2%). This type of cathode material is cost-effective and thermally stable, reducing fire risks [ 64 ]. It has lower energy density but a longer lifespan, making it ideal for mass-market EVs [ 64 ]. It is also environmentally friendly owing to the absence of critical metals. For lithium manganese oxide (LMO), the key component is manganese (10.7%), with high aluminum content (21.7%). This allows it to achieve a balanced energy density and safety [ 65 ]. Manganese reduces costs compared with cobalt, but it has lower cycle life, which limits long-term use. To improve this, it can be combined with nickel manganese cobalt to enhance the performance. Lastly, nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) is composed of nickel (14.8%), cobalt (8.5%), and manganese (5.9%). This type of cathode is commonly used in modern EVs because of its high energy density and improved thermal stability [ 56 ].

sections.heading: Methodologies for the Extraction of Metals from Mixed Cathode Material
paragraphs: LIB recycling methods can be broadly categorized into pyrometallurgical, hydrometallurgical, and direct recycling techniques as well as other emerging methods such as bioleaching and electro-assisted leaching. Bioleaching employs microbes to extract metals, whereas electro-assisted leaching, which reduces acid consumption, is being explored to improve the efficiency and sustainability [ 20 ,  66 ,  67 ] (Fig.  2 ). To address these limitations, pretreatment processes are employed before the purification methods to improve material purity and reduce downstream energy demands.

sections.heading: Pretreatment
paragraphs: Pretreatment processing is crucial for enhancing the recovery efficiency and reducing the energy consumption of the recycling process [ 69 ]. The pretreatment process is essential for effectively separating the LIB components, such as the active material and current collector Al foil, thereby benefiting the subsequent process for leaching of valuable metals [ 70 ]. Popular pretreatment approaches include mechanical, solvent dissolution, heat treatment, and alkali solution approaches [ 70 ]. Mechanical pretreatment involves crushing, screening, magnetic separation, fine crushing, and classification to enrich the LIB granules [ 71 ].

Calcination of the active material in LIBs can remove the carbon and adhesive, reducing the efficiency of chemical leaching [ 72 ,  73 ]. Solvent dissolution pretreatment involves soaking the disassembled cathode material in  N , N -dimethylformamide (DMF) and stirring vigorously at room temperature to remove the cathode material from the Al foil [ 74 ]. DMF with dissolved polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) can be recycled after reaching saturation, reducing the cost of recycling [ 74 ]. Heat pretreatment studies have compared the effects of high-temperature sintering and DMF dissolution on the removal of active substances [ 74 ]. However, high-temperature sintering results in the destruction of the removed active material structure, which cannot be recycled directly [ 74 ]. Alkali dissolution involves using an alkali solution to dissolve the cathode material, separate the cathode material and the current collector (Al foil) [ 75 ,  76 ]. The results showed that nearly 80% of Al can be selectively removed by repeated leaching twice, and the remaining cathode residue can be used in the subsequent acid-leaching process [ 75 ,  76 ].

sections.heading: Hydrometallurgy Processing
paragraphs: The hydrometallurgy process uses reagents such as hydrochloric acid (HCl), nitric acid (HNO 3 ), sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ), phosphoric acid (H 3 PO 4 ), organic acids, and hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) to extract and separate the cathode metals, usually operating below 100 °C; it can yield high-grade cobalt metal or lithium carbonate [ 77 ,  78 – 79 ]. Hydrometallurgy is more suitable for recycling spent LIBs with a single chemical composition, e.g., LCO (LiCoO 2  or lithium cobalt oxide) batteries, where acid leaching can efficiently extract Co and Li because the chemistry is uniform, but with mixed cathodes such as LCO + NMC + LFP, hydrometallurgy struggles owing to the varying metal ratios and extraction requirements [ 80 ,  81 ].

Figure  3  illustrates the hydrometallurgical method for recycling LIBs, which involves several key steps. First, spent LIBs undergo pretreatment. The cathode–anode powder mixture is then transferred to a leaching tank, where it is treated with an acidic solution at temperatures between 40 and 95 °C to dissolve valuable metals such as lithium and cobalt into a liquid phase (leachate). A filter press then separates solid residues, forming a filter cake of unwanted materials [ 82 ,  83 ]. The leachate is then processed in a precipitation tank at room temperature, where a precipitant is added, leading to the formation of cobalt carbonate (CoCO 3 ) and lithium carbonate (Li 2 CO 3 ) [ 82 ,  83 ]. These recovered compounds are further processed in a sintering furnace at 900 °C, where lithium carbonate is converted to lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO 2 ), a crucial cathode material for new LIBs [ 84 ]. This process is more complex than pyrometallurgical approaches but offers higher recovery rates, mild operation conditions, and less environmental pollution [ 84 ]. A recent life cycle assessment (LCA) study found that the most effective hydrometallurgical process can reduce environmental impact by over 50% compared with average recycling processes [ 103 ,  104 ]. This has made it a popular research field and a concern for academia and industry [ 74 ]. After pretreatments, leaching is applied as the next step in the hydrometallurgy process. This step is considered to be the most significant one when it comes to valuable metals recovery as its purpose is to convert the metals present in the cathode material procured in the pretreatment process into an ionic solution [ 105 ]. The leaching media are most often mineral acids (H 2 SO 4 , HCl, and HNO 3 ), alkali, and organic acids. Studies show that inorganic acids are highly effective for the recovery of Co and Li (99%) in the leaching process when applied in optimal conditions, and graphite stays in a solid residue after filtration of the leachate [ 106 ,  107 ].

The main advantage of hydrometallurgy is the possibility to produce new battery precursors from the waste with sufficient purity [ 77 ,  78 – 79 ]. Despite the large demand for chemical reagents, hydrometallurgy allows the use of many solvents for several years and reutilization of several byproducts within the same technology, thus minimizing the overall secondary waste generation [ 108 ]. With future battery legislation and demands for higher material recovery rates, hydrometallurgy is one of the most promising approaches to meet the requirements, but also to create a path to a circular economy in the battery market.

sections.heading: Pyrometallurgical Approaches
paragraphs: In one study, researchers dismantled spent LIBs and calcined the cathodes, which consisted of LiCoO 2  and Al foil, for 2 h, yielding nanocrystalline γ-LiAlO 2 , while Co remained as colored powders in the form of Co 3 O 4  and CoO [ 74 ,  109 ]. The formed nanocrystalline γ-LiAlO 2  was observed under scanning electron microscopy (SEM), with morphology such as coconut particles [ 74 ,  109 ]. It can be used to prepare platinum catalysts [ 74 ,  109 ]. They adopted heat treatment with a high temperature of 150–500 °C for 1 h to separate the active cathode material of LiCoO 2  and the current collector Al foil [ 110 ]. Fe 2 O 3  was added to the removed active material and heated at a high temperature of 1000 °C for 4 h to obtain a mixture of Li 0.5 FeO 4 /CoFeO 4  micron crystals [ 109 ]. Researchers adopted the method where they roasted a mixture of LiCoO 2  (lithium cobalt oxide) and graphite under a nitrogen environment at a temperature of 1000 °C for half an hour, producing a residue with graphite, Co, and Li 2 CO 3  [ 91 ]. The water leaching method was adopted, and the recovery rate of Li, Co, and graphite after the wetting magnetic separation process was reported to be 98.83%, 95.75%, and 91.05%, respectively [ 74 ]. Oxygenizing roasting was found to be significantly effective in separating LiFePO 4  (lithium phosphate iron) cathode material from the Al current collectors owing to the release of fluorine-containing gases such as HF (hydrogen fluoride) [ 74 ].

Oxidative roasting is a process that requires strict temperature control and high energy intensity, leading to potential decreases in Fe recovery in the acid-leaching stage [ 74 ]. The main pyrometallurgical options for recycling spent LiB include pyrolysis, incineration, roasting and smelting [ 74 ]. These processes require high energy intensity and can create secondary air pollution [ 74 ]. Continuous research is needed to reduce energy consumption and secondary waste air pollution during pyrometallurgical recycling processes. sections.heading: Direct Recycling
paragraphs: Direct recycling of LIB cathodes is all about reinstating spent cathode resources to their natural structure and configuration to permit their reutilization in new battery manufacture, thus sustaining the cathode’s framework [ 128 ]. This method is mainly advantageous for highly valuable cathodes such as lithium cobalt oxide and nickel–manganese–cobalt variants because it preserves their electrochemical properties with insignificant processing [ 56 ]. Separating cathode components (CAMs) from aluminum foil or polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder is typically done using methods such as dissolution or decomposition [ 129 ]. Hansen solubility parameters and PVDF solubility behaviors were investigated in 46 solvents, and several solvents were tested for their capacity to separate cathode components while recycling LIBs. NMP was found to be the most efficient solvent, followed by  N , N -dimethylacetamide (DMAC),  N , N -dimethylformamide (DMF),  N , N -dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and ethanol [ 130 ]. Ultrasonic technology was used to improve the process’s efficiency, with ideal parameters being 240 W of ultrasonic power, a 70 °C temperature, and a 90-min reaction time [ 130 ].

Researchers are redefining recycling models and extraction methods through various studies. it was discovered that fluorine reacts with Mn and Li in NMC cathodes, causing surface decomposition and lithium loss. Their breakthrough involved adding excess LiOH·H 2 O during heating, which sequestered fluorine by forming a protective LiF–MnO x  phase [ 131 ]. This simple step preserved the cathode’s structural integrity, enabling 95% capacity retention after 100 cycles, a marked improvement over untreated samples [ 131 ]. With mixed cathode waste (e.g., NMC111 + LMO) becoming common, Folayan et al. [ 132 ] pioneered a multistage froth flotation process [ 52 ,  132 ]. By tuning the pH and surfactants used, they achieved 95% purity for both NMC111 (froth product) and LMO (tailing product). The key to success was exploiting differences in particle hydrophobicity, a strategy now adopted for other blends such as NMC–LFP, transforming spent polycrystalline NMC111 into high-performance single-crystal NMC622 by solid-state reaction with NiO [ 133 ]. The upcycled cathodes delivered 20% higher capacity (178 mAh/g at 0.1 °C) and superior cycling stability (85% retention after 200 cycles at 5 °C). This approach not only avoided costly leaching but also upgraded the cathode chemistry [ 27 ,  134 ].

In one study, researchers demonstrated that hydrothermal relithiation (4 M LiOH, 200 °C) combined with solid-state annealing (800 °C) could restore NMC cathodes to ~ 98% of their original capacity [ 27 ,  134 ]. However, the consistency varied across chemistries; LFP showed faster Li diffusion than NMC, while LCO required precise oxygen control to prevent Co 3+  reduction. Despite progress, Piątek et al. [ 135 ] highlighted unresolved hurdles, which include mechanical cracks and Ni/Li mixing in NMC, reducing recyclability, lithium loss, and residual Al/F contamination, and necessitating additional purification steps. These studies collectively reveal that, while thermal binder modification, flotation separation, and solid-state upcycling are viable for specific cathodes, a universal direct recycling protocol remains elusive. Future work must address chemistry-specific protocols, e.g., LFP versus NMC, especially when it comes to pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy extraction methods, because impurity limits for direct reuse into making other batteries and catalysts in other manufacturing industries. By bridging these gaps, recycling methods such as direct recycling could shift from laboratory-scale promise to industrial reality. Research is still being developed and most of it is under laboratory scale, which is promising to provide new innovations in extraction methods and sustainability in LIB recycling.

sections.heading: New Developments and Innovations in LIB Extraction and Recycling Methodologies
paragraphs: Recent advancements in LIB recycling focus on improving recovery efficiency, reducing chemical waste, and optimizing economic feasibility. Emerging technologies such as electrochemical extraction, bioleaching, and closed-loop recycling systems are gaining traction [ 20 ]. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven material sorting, green solvents, and automation in dismantling processes are also contributing to more sustainable and cost-effective recycling pathways [ 147 ]. Leading companies and research institutions across Asia, Europe, and North America are actively developing next-generation recycling solutions to align with this [ 148 ].

sections.heading: Deep Eutectic Solvents (DES), Ionic Liquids, Mechanochemical Extraction, and Functionalized Adsorbents
paragraphs: Deep eutectic solvents (DES) have emerged as a promising green alternative to conventional mineral acid leaching for recovering critical metals from spent LIBs. DES are formed by mixing a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), typically choline chloride, with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) such as urea, ethylene glycol, or oxalic acid, resulting in a solvent with a significantly lower melting point than either individual component. Studies have demonstrated that choline chloride-based DES systems can achieve extraction efficiencies exceeding 90% for Li and Co from LiCoO 2  cathodes at mild temperatures (60–80 °C), while generating far less toxic waste compared with H 2 SO 4 -based leaching [ 144 ]. Their tunable physicochemical properties, low volatility, and biodegradability make them attractive for sustainable LIB recycling at scale. Ionic liquid (IL)-based leaching represents another frontier approach, using thermally stable, nonvolatile salts in liquid state at room temperature to selectively solubilize transition metals. Hydrophobic ILs such as [P66614][Cl] have demonstrated high selectivity for Co 2+  and Ni 2+  over Li  + , enabling targeted metal separation without the need for additional solvent extraction steps [ 149 ]. Mechanochemical-assisted extraction involves high-energy ball milling of spent cathode materials, which induces lattice strain, reduces particle size, and activates the surface of cathode oxides prior to leaching. This pretreatment significantly reduces the amount of acid reagent required and shortens the leaching times, with studies reporting up to 95% Co and Ni recovery when using dilute H 2 SO 4  following mechanochemical activation [ 125 ]. Finally, functionalized adsorbents including ion-imprinted polymers (IIPs) and metal–organic framework (MOF)-based materials offer highly selective recovery of individual metal ions from complex leachate solutions. Li + -selective IIPs have demonstrated adsorption capacities exceeding 30 mg/g with selectivity coefficients several orders of magnitude above competing ions, representing a viable path to battery-grade lithium recovery without multistage precipitation.

sections.heading: Bio-extraction and Microbial Metal Recovery
paragraphs: Bio-extraction has attracted attention as a sustainable alternative for metal recovery from spent LIB cathodes [ 150 ]. Certain bacteria and fungi have been found to produce organic acids that facilitate the dissolution of lithium, cobalt, and other metals [ 151 ]. Studies indicate that microbial-assisted leaching can achieve recovery rates comparable to conventional acid leaching while minimizing hazardous waste generation [ 152 ]. Bio-extraction studies on the recovery of metals using bacteria and fungal species have provided promising results [ 152 ]. They can become a promising, cost-effective technique without using harsh chemicals and higher temperatures. However, very few microbes (Fig.  4 ) have been reported to have such functional properties, and their yield is significantly lower [ 150 ,  152 ]. Fig. 4 The bioleaching process flow for recycling cathode metals (specifically nickel, manganese, and cobalt, or NMC) from LIBs using  A. ferrooxidans  for LIB metal extraction

Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans  is a bacterium that oxidizes iron/sulfur, producing acids (e.g., sulfuric acid) that dissolve metals from the cathode material [ 153 ]. Other microbes include  A. thiooxidans  and fungi such as  Aspergillus niger  that can also be used to leach metals via organic (citric and oxalic) acids.  Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans  oxidizes Fe 2+  (ferrous iron) to Fe 3+  (ferric iron), electron donor, and sulfur compounds [ 153 ]. Fe 3+  acts as a strong oxidant, breaking down NMC cathodes, while the sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ) lowers the pH (~ 1.5–2.5), which enhances the metal dissolution [ 154 ]. Optimal conditions of this process are 30–35 °C, aerobic, and acidic pH (1.5–3.0). This process is, however, sensitive to high metal concentrations; e.g., > 10 g/L Li can inhibit growth, and it has slow kinetics that can take days to weeks [ 153 ,  154 ].

Aspergillus niger  is a fungi that is used in organic acid leaching as it produces organic acids such as citric, oxalic, and gluconic acids that chelate metals, while citric acid also forms soluble complexes with Co and Ni [ 101 ,  155 ]. It works at milder pH (~ 3–6) and ambient temperatures (20–30 °C), and its acidity reduces corrosion risks.  Aspergillus niger  can leach 70–90% of Co, Ni, and Mn from cathodes in 7–14 days and its advantage over bacteria is that it tolerates higher metal concentrations [ 156 ,  157 ]. However, challenges such as bacterial inhibition at high pulp densities, uncertain catalytic mechanisms, and optimization of organic acid production require further investigation to enhance the commercial viability of bioleaching-based recycling processes.

There is also growing research on other recycling and metal extraction technologies, as shown in Table  9 . These methods primarily belong to the electrochemical methods category of LIB recycling. They offer high selectivity and efficiency in extracting specific battery materials. Some are sustainable alternatives, e.g., ultrasonic-assisted, electrochemical leaching, that reduce chemical consumption compared with traditional acid-based leaching. In addition, some techniques are still under research and development, while others, such as solvent extraction and electrodeposition, are already used in some commercial LIB recycling operations [ 156 ]. These methods differ from other traditional recycling approaches, such as pyrometallurgy, mechanical pretreatment, and direct recycling, that rely on high-temperature processing or physical separation rather than chemical reactions. sections.heading: Reparation and Reuse of Recovered Metals in Different Industries
paragraphs: Efficient recovery and reuse of these metals from LIBs is critical for establishing a circular economy, reducing the environmental impacts of mining, and securing supply chains for multiple industries [ 174 ]. The petroleum, oil and gas, and renewable energy sectors can particularly benefit from repurposing these recovered metals, as they rely heavily on many of the same materials [ 175 ]. Advanced recycling techniques now enable the extraction of high-purity metals suitable for reintegration into industrial processes and next-generation technologies [ 30 ]

sections.heading: Applications in the Petroleum, and Oil and Gas Industry
paragraphs: The petroleum sector requires robust, high-performance materials for refining, drilling, and infrastructure. Recovered metals from LIB cathodes can serve multiple functions in this industry while reducing reliance on primary mining [ 176 ]. One of the most valuable applications is in catalysts for oil refining processes. Cobalt and nickel recovered from spent nickel–manganese–cobalt (NMC) batteries can be processed into active catalyst materials for hydrodesulfurization (HDS), a critical step in producing low-sulfur fuels [ 36 ]. These metals, when supported on other substrates, demonstrate comparable catalytic activity to virgin materials, enabling cleaner fuel production while lowering the carbon footprint of refinery operations [ 177 ].

Beyond catalysis, these metals are essential for manufacturing corrosion-resistant alloys used in pipelines, offshore drilling rigs, and refinery equipment [ 178 ]. Nickel is a key component in stainless steels and superalloys that must withstand extreme conditions, including high pressures, temperatures, and exposure to corrosive substances [ 178 ]. Recycled nickel from LIBs can be alloyed with chromium and molybdenum to produce materials that meet industry standards for durability and performance. This not only conserves resources but also reduces the energy-intensive processing required for virgin nickel production [ 179 ]. Additionally, lithium compounds recovered from battery recycling have applications in drilling fluids, where they act as rheology modifiers to stabilize the fluid under high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) conditions. Lithium hydroxide (LiOH) and lithium carbonate (Li 2 CO 3 ) help maintain the viscosity and thermal stability of drilling muds, preventing wellbore instability. Given the increasing difficulty of accessing conventional lithium reserves, recycled lithium offers a sustainable alternative for the oilfield chemicals market [ 180 ].

sections.heading: Integration into Renewable Energy Technologies
paragraphs: The renewable energy sector is another major beneficiary of recycled LIB metals, particularly in wind, solar and next-generation energy storage systems. Wind turbine generators traditionally rely on rare-earth permanent magnets containing neodymium (Nd) and dysprosium (Dy), which are subject to supply-chain vulnerabilities [ 181 ]. However, research has shown that cobalt and manganese recovered from spent LIBs can be used in alternative magnet formulations, reducing the dependence on critical rare-earth elements [ 181 ]. These alloys exhibit sufficient magnetic properties for use in direct-drive turbines, contributing to more sustainable wind energy infrastructure.

In solar photovoltaics (PV), nickel and cobalt play roles in advanced cell architectures, including perovskite solar cells (PSCs) and thin-film technologies [ 182 ]. Nickel oxide (NiO), derived from recycled LIB cathodes, has been successfully employed as a hole-transport layer in PSCs, achieving efficiencies comparable to those using virgin materials [ 183 ]. Similarly, cobalt-based compounds enhance the stability and charge transport properties of dye-sensitized and organic solar cells. By incorporating recycled metals, the solar industry can lower its environmental footprint while maintaining high performance [ 184 ]. The energy storage sector also benefits from closed-loop metal recovery, particularly in the development of next-generation batteries [ 184 ]. Recycled lithium can be processed into high-purity lithium salts for solid-state electrolytes, which are key to safer, higher-energy-density batteries. Meanwhile, manganese and iron recovered from LFP and NMC cathodes are being explored for use in sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), an emerging alternative to LIBs [ 22 ]. These metals can be incorporated into Prussian blue analogs (PBAs) and other cathode materials, providing a cost-effective and sustainable pathway for grid-scale storage solutions.

sections.heading: Relithiation for Direct Battery Regeneration
paragraphs: Relithiation is a process that aims to restore the cathode’s initial composition and electrochemical performance without altering its structure [ 185 ]. It is crucial for resource conservation, cost-effectiveness, and addressing the growing demand for raw materials in the rapidly expanding battery industry. Beyond extracting metals for external industries, relithiation enables direct regeneration of cathode materials for reuse in new LIBs [ 186 ]. Techniques such as hydrothermal LiOH infusion (180–220 °C) or molten salt treatments (300–500 °C) restore the lithium stoichiometry while preserving the cathode’s crystal structure [ 187 ]. This approach is especially viable for low-degradation NMC or LCO cathodes, achieving > 95% capacity recovery. For severely degraded materials, partial relithiation still improves downstream metal extraction efficiency, critical for supplying high-purity Co/Ni to catalysts or Mn to steel alloys. However, scalability and energy inputs require further optimization to compete with conventional hydrometallurgy [ 86 ]. Several methods exist for relithiating degraded cathode active materials (CAMs), each with distinct advantages and limitations. Solid-state sintering, typically using Li 2 CO 3  at 800–900 °C under inert atmosphere, effectively restores layered structures but demands high energy [ 188 ]. Hydrothermal relithiation employs LiOH solutions (180–220 °C and 5–20 h) for uniform lithium distribution, though requiring subsequent annealing [ 27 ]. The ionic liquid method operates at moderate temperatures (150 °C) using LiBr in ionic liquids, offering precise control but facing cost barriers [ 149 ]. Molten salt approaches (300–500 °C) using eutectic mixtures such as LiOH–LiNO 3  combine relithiation with impurity removal at reduced temperatures. Electrochemical methods enable direct Li +  insertion via applied voltage (0.5–1.5 V), producing zero chemical waste but requiring complex setups [ 189 ].

sections.heading: Synergies with Petroleum and Renewable Energy Applications
paragraphs: Relithiation supports metal recovery for nonbattery industries in two key ways. First, it provides a lithium supply for oilfield chemicals, as relithiation, which can be diverted to drilling fluids or grease production if battery-grade purity is not required [ 190 ]. This avoids competition with the battery sector, as lower-grade lithium is acceptable for industrial uses. Relithiated cathodes (e.g., NMC) show more consistent leaching behavior, which allows for better-controlled manganese recovery for wind turbine steel alloys and higher-purity nickel and cobalt for refinery catalysts with fewer impurities from incomplete delithiation, and it improves metal recovery for catalysts and alloys [ 173 ]. Relithiation is promising, but its integration faces challenges, including high-temperature processes such as solid-state sintering at 800 °C (which may offset sustainability benefits if powered by fossil fuels), chemistry-specific limits (as methods optimized for NMC may not work for LFP or NCA cathodes without customization), and lastly that most relithiation techniques remain laboratory scale, requiring pilot plants to test compatibility with industrial metal recovery processes [ 32 ]. Despite these promising applications, several challenges must be addressed to fully realize the potential of metal repatriation.

One major hurdle is achieving the ultrahigh purity required for certain industrial uses, particularly in catalysts and high-performance alloys. While hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical recycling methods can recover metals efficiently, additional purification steps such as solvent extraction or electrochemical refining may be necessary to meet stringent industry specifications. Economic factors also play a significant role. The cost of recycling and refining metals must compete with primary production, which is currently more established and, in some cases, cheaper. However, as regulatory pressures increase and mining becomes more constrained owing to environmental and geopolitical factors, recycled metals are expected to gain a competitive edge. Policies promoting extended producer responsibility (EPR) and subsidies for sustainable material sourcing could further accelerate adoption.

Another critical consideration is the development of standardized guidelines for using recycled metals in high-stakes applications, such as aerospace or medical-grade alloys. Collaborative efforts between battery recyclers, material scientists, and industry stakeholders will be essential to establish certification protocols that ensure reliability and performance.

sections.heading: Research Outlooks
paragraphs: Research on the recycling of LIB is in its infancy, and the research gaps identified in this review render it a fertile field of research. The global push to increase renewable energy in the energy mix globally, the use of EVs, the establishment of circular economies, and the promotion of sustainable development have led to a rise in battery usage. This has created an urgent need to develop ecofriendly methods for the extraction and recycling of spent batteries that are both commercially feasible and sustainable.

This review identifies concerns regarding the environmental impact of acid leaching and the generation of secondary waste streams, necessitating further research to bridge this knowledge gap. The variable material composition in batteries has complicated the development of a one-size-fits-all recycling method; thus, several methods were reviewed, and although hydrometallurgy was identified as a promising approach to create a path to a circular economy in the battery market, research is needed to minimize its waste output. In the pyrometallurgy recycling process, ongoing research is essential to reduce lithium loss in slag, minimize energy consumption, and reduce air pollution from secondary waste during recycling. There is also a significant gap that needs to be addressed by research, particularly regarding chemistry-specific protocols for pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy extraction methods. This is important because impurity limits affect direct reuse in the production of other batteries and catalysts in various manufacturing industries.

For the direct recycling process, further investigation is required to tackle outstanding challenges, including mechanical cracks and the mixing of nickel and lithium in nickel–manganese–cobalt (NMC) materials. These issues contribute to decreased recyclability, lithium loss, and contamination from residual aluminum and fluoride. Addressing them will make it possible to scale up from the laboratory to industrial scale. The review has also revealed that, while methods such as thermal binder modification, flotation separation, and solid-state upcycling are effective for certain cathodes, a universal direct recycling protocol has not been achieved. Research that focuses on upscaling relithiation techniques from laboratory and pilot scales to industrial scale is necessary to test their compatibility with industrial metal recovery processes.

Among the various metal extraction methods reviewed, bio-extraction stands out as the most environmentally friendly approach. However, several challenges need to be addressed to enhance the commercial viability of bioleaching-based recycling processes. These challenges include bacterial inhibition at high pulp densities, unclear catalytic mechanisms, and the optimization of organic acid production. Further investigation into these areas is necessary. Another important factor to consider is the need for standardized guidelines regarding the use of recycled metals in high-stakes applications, such as aerospace or medical-grade alloys. To ensure reliability and performance, further research and collaboration among battery recyclers, material scientists, and industry stakeholders will be essential for establishing certification protocols.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This review contributes to the body of knowledge by shifting the focus from established recycling methods and standard metallurgical processes to a sustainable, circular-economy-driven paradigm that prioritizes biotechnological and green innovations for spent LIBs. It emphasizes a significant shift toward biotechnological solutions, particularly bioleaching, as a primary strategy for sustainable development and explores how these methods align with global decarbonization frameworks to create closed-loop battery economies. The potential of green leaching technologies, including DES, ionic-liquid-based leaching, and mechanochemical-assisted extraction, which are not yet standard in industrial workflows, was shown. The review provides an in-depth comparison of direct recycling methods, reinstating cathode resources to their original structure against traditional destructive methods, with specific innovations such as froth flotation and hydrothermal relithiation highlighted. Bio-hydrometallurgical analysis helped to distinguish between bacterial and fungal bio-extraction and highlighted that, while bacteria such as  A. ferrooxidans  are effective, fungi such as  Aspergillus niger  offer superior tolerance to high metal concentrations. The review also revealed that, while traditional pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy remain the industry standards, they are constrained by high energy consumption and the production of secondary waste. The research’s other notable contribution is connecting laboratory-scale innovations with industrial applications, offering a roadmap for returning high-purity metals to sectors such as renewable energy and the oil and gas industry.

Additionally, it was shown that the shift toward a circular economy, in which materials are reused in new batteries and other applications, is vital to the long-term sustainability of the industry. Encouraging manufacturers to design batteries with recycling in mind and fostering decentralized recycling hubs will also play a key role in making LIB recycling more efficient and widely adopted. Regulatory frameworks will need to evolve alongside technological advancements to incentivize recycling, particularly by mandating recycling rates and creating economic incentives for the use of recycled materials. The future of LIB cathode recycling holds great promise, but realizing this potential will require continued innovation, cross-sector collaboration, and robust policy support. Research and industry development in this field must focus on overcoming existing challenges while embracing the opportunities offered by new technologies and sustainable practices.
